questions.question:
Study this full HTTP request-response cycle for a browser page load. At which step is the TCP connection first established?

User types URL → Browser checks cache → DNS Lookup → ??? → TLS Handshake → HTTP GET / → Server → 200 OK → Browser renders

values: Step 1: User types https://example.com
Step 2: Browser checks local DNS cache
Step 3: DNS resolver returns IP address (e.g. 93.184.216.34)
Step 4: Browser initiates TCP 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK)
Step 5: TLS handshake over established TCP connection
Step 6: HTTP GET / sent over encrypted tunnel
Step 7: Server responds 200 OK with HTML
Step 8: Browser parses HTML, fetches sub-resources, renders page

options: Step 2 — DNS cache check establishes the TCP connection
Step 5 — TLS handshake creates the TCP connection
Step 4 — TCP 3-way handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK) establishes the connection before TLS
Step 6 — the HTTP GET triggers TCP connection creation
questions.answer: Step 4 — TCP 3-way handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK) establishes the connection before TLS

429 means the request payload is too large; the client should reduce data size
429 is a server error — the client has no recourse
questions.answer: 429 Too Many Requests means the client has exceeded the rate limit; the Retry-After header tells the client to wait 60 seconds before retrying

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between HTTP PUT and HTTP PATCH methods?

PUT replaces the entire resource with the request payload; PATCH applies a partial update — only the fields provided in the request are changed
PATCH creates a new resource; PUT updates an existing one
PUT is idempotent; PATCH is not allowed in REST APIs
questions.answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with the request payload; PATCH applies a partial update — only the fields provided in the request are changed

questions.answer: Force all future requests to this domain and its subdomains to use HTTPS only for the next 31536000 seconds (1 year) — even if the user types http://
